The O’Keeffe family at Blackrock, 1939. Back, left to right: Maura (later Greene), Martin, Sarah Catherine “Eda” in her mother’s arms, and May. Front, left to right: Rickard “Rick”, John Joseph “Jack”, and Edmund “Ed”. Frederick, who died at three in 1928, is missing from it.

okSarah.name: Sarah Elizabeth O’Keeffe
vitals: Richard O’Keeffe & Elizabeth Mary Davis Foley

bio.t: Her eldest son John Butler (1922–1994) kept the Troy Times cutting about the box of shamrock sent from Blackrock to Joseph Davis Foley. His widow Cait Butler gave it to John Brennan and Miriam O’Keeffe in 2012, and it is one of the documents that opened this research.

okMaryInfant.name: Mary O’Keeffe
vitals: Plot FG 143.5, Glasnevin, with her grandmother Elizabeth Davis Foley

bio.t: She lived one day and was buried with her grandmother, who had died six years earlier. The Glasnevin record of that grave carries both of them.

okJack.name: John Joseph “Jack” O’Keeffe
vitals: Martin J. O’Keeffe & Mary J. O’Reilly
Catherine M. · Martin · John Dermot · Miriam Joan

bio.t: The reason any of this survives. As executor of his uncle Eoin’s will he took charge of Eoin’s papers, and kept them until his own death in June 2012. Josephine’s two letters of 1931 were among them.

After Jack died the papers passed to his daughter Miriam, who in 2026 donated the bulk of them to the National Library of Ireland (MS Acc. 11,221) and the Josephine letters separately to Imirce: the Kirby A. Miller Collection at the University of Galway, where they can now be read by anyone.
He is the boy in the middle of the front row in 1939, twelve years old and grinning. Seventy-three years later his daughter would place his uncle’s papers in the National Library of Ireland.

photos.cap: The O’Keeffe family at Blackrock, 1939. Back, left to right: Maura (later Greene), Martin, Sarah Catherine “Eda” in her mother’s arms, and May. Front, left to right: Rickard “Rick”, John Joseph “Jack”, and Edmund “Ed”. Frederick, who died at three in 1928, is missing from it.

okMiriam.name: Miriam O’Keeffe
okMiriam.role: Jack’s daughter · great-great-granddaughter of John Hogan Foley
vitals: John Joseph “Jack” O’Keeffe & Joan T. Aherne
Eoin O’Keeffe’s papers to the National Library of Ireland, 2026 · MS Acc. 11,221
Josephine Benson’s 1931 letters to Imirce, University of Galway, 2026
The headstone over Eliza Davis Foley’s grave at Glasnevin

bio.t: It is her Foley line. She inherited Eoin’s papers from her father Jack and placed them in two national collections in 2026 rather than keeping them, which is why Josephine’s handwriting is now readable from anywhere in the world.
She also holds the undated brochure describing Foley’s Universal Angular Instrument, the only surviving description of what John Hogan Foley actually built.
Her husband John Brennan compiled the Foley, Gore and O’Keeffe genealogies this record depends on.
Named in his son Daniel’s 2015 obituary as the late Arthur Hamilton. Beyond that, nothing is documented: no dates, no birthplace, no occupation.

Dan was born in Cambridge in 1925 and raised in Somerville, so Arthur’s records should sit in Middlesex County. The marriage record to Agnes is the document that matters most, because it will name both sets of parents and settle the question below.
Whether he was an immigrant or American-born is unknown. The 1930 and 1940 federal censuses for Cambridge and Somerville would answer it.

h_agnes.name: Agnes Frances Hamilton
vitals: Hamilton — she was born a Hamilton and married a Hamilton

bio.t: Her maiden name was also Hamilton. That is not a transcription error; it is how her son’s obituary records her.

It means one of two things. Either a marriage between cousins, which was common enough in tight immigrant communities, or two entirely unrelated Hamilton families converging in greater Boston. The two possibilities lead to completely different ancestries, and the tree cannot go further back on this line until it is resolved.
One document settles it: the Arthur and Agnes marriage record, which will name both sets of parents. If the fathers are brothers, it is a cousin marriage. If they are unconnected, it is coincidence.

h_clarence.name: Clarence Fairburn
vitals: Claire Ardell · George · Stewart · Douglas · Donald, and at least one more

bio.t: Father of Claire, who was born in Cambridge in 1929, so he was living there by the late 1920s. He raised at least five children and probably more: Claire’s 2022 obituary names Fairburn nieces and nephews who cannot be accounted for by her four known brothers.

Fairburn is a Scottish Borders surname. Claire’s pride in her Scottish ancestry was real enough that she debuted at the Scottish Ball, and the 1930 census for Cambridge would establish whether Clarence was the immigrant or a generation removed.
Her maiden name adds a fourth surname to this side: Hamilton, Fairburn, Stewart, and whichever Hamiltons Agnes came from.

Her name carried forward. One of her sons was christened Stewart Fairburn, the mother’s maiden name used as a first name, which is a common Scottish practice and a useful genealogical marker. It is the kind of detail that makes a line traceable.

h_dan.name: Daniel John Hamilton
vitals: 11 April 2015, at home on Oakridge Avenue, North Attleboro · aged 89
USS Colahan · USS Prichett · USS Chauncey · USS Swenning · USS Enterprise
Asiatic-Pacific Campaign ribbon with three battle stars · Philippine Liberation ribbon
Texas Instruments, Attleboro — thirty years, retiring as superintendent

bio.t: Cambridge born, Somerville raised, and at sea before he was twenty. He enlisted on 2 September 1943 and served until April 1946.

Five ships, and one of them is not like the others. Four are Pacific ships. The Colahan fought at Guam, the Palaus, Leyte, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. The Prichett took a bomb hole and later a kamikaze at Okinawa, and held a Navy Unit Commendation for radar picket duty there. The Chauncey was at Wake and Rabaul. The Enterprise was the most decorated American warship of the war.

The Swenning was a destroyer escort, and she spent 1944 in the North Atlantic hunting U-boats with the escort carrier Bogue. She did not reach the Pacific until 30 August 1945, after the surrender, and then trained submarines out of Guam until January 1946 before sailing home to Boston, arriving 26 February. Dan was released that April. She may well have brought him home.

Three battle stars, not eight. Battle stars follow the sailor and not the ship: one for each operation you were personally aboard for. The Colahan earned eight, the Prichett eight, the Chauncey seven. Dan had three, which means he joined the Pacific war late and moved between ships. The Philippine Liberation ribbon is the hard constraint, since it required presence in Philippine waters between 17 October 1944 and 3 September 1945. The likeliest three are Leyte, Iwo Jima and Okinawa.

Two open questions about the shape of his life. Five ships in thirty-one months is unusual for a deck rating and typical of a technical specialist. Two of his ships did radar picket work, he went to MIT, and he spent thirty years at Texas Instruments. Navy radar to MIT to semiconductors is one continuous line rather than three unrelated facts, but it is a hypothesis. And it is not established whether MIT came after the war on the GI Bill or during it under the Navy V-12 programme, for which MIT was a host school.

His Navy personnel file survives at the National Personnel Records Center in St Louis. Navy records were untouched by the 1973 fire. As next of kin the family can request it, and it would give the rating, the transfer dates, and the three operations behind those stars by name.
He died at home on Oakridge Avenue in April 2015. His granddaughter’s brother named a son Bowen Daniel in 2022.

bio.t: The other Foley. An alderman and later Mayor of Columbus, Georgia, and the man who in 1897 visited Troy, New York and was reported as the guest of “his cousin, J. D. Foley.”

His wedding notice calls him a rising young business man of the city who by his gentlemanly deportment and strict integrity had won the respect and confidence of the best citizens. Adele Springer was a brunette, married in cream brocaded satin trimmed with Spanish lace, orange blossoms and lilies of the valley, wearing pearls and diamonds. Among the bridal attendants: Miss Maggie Foley.

A later cutting records him and Adele returning from Belmont, North Carolina, where their son Joe was at college, and attending the silver jubilee of Bishop Haid at the cathedral — a three-day event with Cardinal Gibbons of Baltimore present, a Supreme Court Justice, several governors, and about a hundred and fifty bishops, abbots and priests.

Why he matters here. These cuttings sit in a scrapbook in the Frank Foley Family Papers at the Hargrett Library, University of Georgia — his family’s archive, not ours. On the same page, in the same hand, is Joseph Davis Foley’s wedding notice from Troy. The Georgia Foleys kept track of the New York Foleys and pasted their news alongside their own. His descendants believe John Hogan Foley may have been a brother of their Daniel Mathew Foley, and that he may be the John Foley born 4 May 1804, possibly in Tipperary, who appears on a handwritten list of Daniel’s siblings in the family album. The relationship is not proven and the 1804 date sits awkwardly against 1817.
John Brennan’s own observation, having colourised the portrait, is that he looks a great deal like his cousin Joseph Davis Foley.

bio.t: He is named on the headstone that John Brennan and Miriam O’Keeffe raised over Eliza Davis Foley’s grave: Also interred William Graham, died 22nd August 1863, aged 30 years.

Answered. He is no relation. Prospect Cemetery at Glasnevin reused the plot when Eliza was buried in it in 1883, twenty years after Graham went into the ground. That was ordinary practice in Victorian Dublin.

When John and Miriam found the unmarked plot and learned who was in it, they put his name on the stone anyway, alongside Eliza and her infant granddaughter. Their reasoning, in John’s words, was that nobody should be in an unmarked grave and they knew he was buried there too.

pierre_tremblay.name: Pierre Tremblay
pierre_tremblay.role: Brittany’s 9× great-grandfather · the ancestor of every Tremblay in North America
vitals: c. 1626, La Filonnière, parish of Saint-Malo, Randonnai, Perche, France

bio.t: This is where the Tremblay name comes from. Not this family’s alone. Tremblay is the most common surname in Québec, and the overwhelming majority of the people carrying it descend from this one man and one woman.

He was born about 1626 at a place called La Filonnière in the parish of Saint-Malo at Randonnai, in the Perche, now part of the commune of Tourouvre au Perche in the Orne. His father, a ploughman, died when Pierre was about fourteen.

At twenty-one he signed an engagement contract at Tourouvre on 9 April 1647, binding himself to three years’ work in Canada for Noël Juchereau at seventy-five livres a year, with food and the crossing both ways found. He walked or rode the three hundred and thirty kilometres south to La Rochelle and boarded La Marguerite on 6 June 1647. He had almost certainly never seen the sea.

Ten years pass with no trace of him in the record. Then, on 19 September 1657, he and Ozanne Achon sat down with a notary to draw up a marriage contract. Neither of them could write their own name. Both made a mark. They married a fortnight later at Notre-Dame de Québec.

He took two arpents at L’Ange-Gardien in 1659 and farmed there. In 1678 he leased the Québec seminary’s farm at Baie-Saint-Paul for five years. He died in April 1687, and there is a statue at L’Ange-Gardien raised in 1957 for the three hundredth anniversary of the marriage.

And one coincidence worth sitting with. The notary who drew that contract, Claude Auber of the Seigneury of Beaupré, appears to be the same Claude Auber who is an ancestor on the other side of this family, through Marion Audette’s LaRochelle and Lemieux line. If so, in September 1657 one of Brittany’s ancestors wrote out the marriage contract of two others, and the three lines would not meet again for nearly three hundred years.

bio.t: She crossed the Atlantic in 1657, at twenty-four, as one of the filles à marier — the women recruited to New France before the state-funded filles du roi programme began, who came at their own or a sponsor’s expense to marry settlers.
She married Pierre within weeks of arriving. Like him, she could not sign her name.
She fell seriously ill in 1707 and appears on the admissions list of the Hôtel-Dieu at Québec on 20 June that year. She was buried on Christmas Eve, having outlived her husband by twenty years.

This record already contained a dozen filles du roi on the Audette side. She is the earlier kind, and she is on the Tremblay side, which until July 2026 had no documented ancestors at all beyond Massachusetts.

bio.t: The eldest son of the immigrant, and a considerable rise in one generation. His father crossed as an indentured ploughman who could not write his name. Pierre held Les Éboulements, one of the largest seigneuries in the colony.

His first marriage lasted nine months. On 3 November 1683 at Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré he married Marie Madeleine Simard dite Lombrette, who was sixteen. Their son Pierre was born on 14 August 1684. She died on the 24th, ten days later, and was buried at Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré on the 27th. She was seventeen years and seven months old.

The child lived fifteen months and died at L’Ange-Gardien on 15 November 1685. That is the same date, at the same parish, as Pierre’s second marriage. Several independent sources give both. It may be a registration artefact rather than a single day’s events, but as the records stand he buried his son and married Marie Roussin on the same day in the same church.

He had fifteen children with Marie Roussin and was survived by her and by twelve of them. He died in October 1736 and was buried at Petite-Rivière-Saint-François. This family descends from the second marriage. The first left no descendants at all.
She was sixteen when she married Pierre, a widower of twenty-five whose first wife and infant son were both dead. Fifteen children followed. She outlived him by nearly twenty years.
The Roussins and Tremblays were already entangled. Her father Nicolas Roussin married Pierre’s sister Marie-Madeleine Tremblay, so her stepmother was her husband’s sister.

A correction worth recording. At least one published source describes her as a fille du roi. She was not. The filles du roi were women sent from France between 1663 and 1673; Marie Roussin was born at L’Ange-Gardien in 1669 and never crossed anything. This record has a dozen genuine filles du roi on the Audette side and she is not one of them.
One link in the chain of seven marriage records that connects Louis Alcime Tremblay back to Pierre Tremblay and Ozanne Achon. Married in 1724.

bio.t: Married Marie Anne Victoire Girard at Baie-Saint-Paul on 12 January 1757, two years before the fall of Québec. The register describes him as the son of the late Nicolas Tremblay.
He was still alive thirty-six years later to stand godfather at the baptism of his grandson Marcel, which is how this record knows the generation between them is right.

bio.t: The one link in this chain with no surviving image. Généalogie Québec records his marriage to Marie Bouchard at Baie-Saint-Paul on 8 July 1787 and names his parents, but the register page has never been scanned.
His son Marcel’s baptism of 1793 supplies the proof anyway: the godfather is entered as Louis Marie Tremblay, the child’s grandfather. The generation stands on that.

One oddity worth recording. Julia has found baptisms at Baie-Saint-Paul for eight children of Louis Marie Tremblay and Marie Anne Victoire Girard — Aimé (1762), Marie Anne Victoire (1765), Pierre (1766), Jean Baptiste (1768), Emerentienne Marie Agnes (1770), Ursule (1774), Jean (1776) and Antoine (1779) — but no baptism for a Louis. Either his record is lost, or he was baptised in another parish.
Married into the Tremblay line in 1787.

marcel_tremblay.name: Marcel Tremblay
vitals: Marie Louise Tremblay, widow of Michel Bouchard, his grandmother

bio.t: Born on the evening of 18 September 1793 and baptised the next morning at Baie-Saint-Paul, son of Louis Tremblay and Marie Bouchard.

This baptism closes a documentary gap. Généalogie Québec records a marriage of Louis Tremble and Marie Bouchard at Baie-Saint-Paul on 8 July 1787, naming his parents as Louis Marie Tremble and Marie Anne Girard, but no scan of that register page survives. Marcel’s baptism supplies the link independently: the godfather is entered as Louis Marie Tremblay, grandfather of the child. The generation is confirmed without needing the missing marriage record.

The godmother is Marie Louise Tremblay, widow of Michel Bouchard, and the child’s grandmother on the other side — which means Marie Bouchard’s own mother was a Tremblay. The two families had been marrying into each other for generations.
Both godparents at this christening were the baby’s grandparents, one from each side.

bio.t: She was married at sixteen, gave birth at seventeen, and died ten days afterwards. Her son outlived her by fifteen months. Neither of them left descendants, and a French account of the family disposes of her entire marriage in four words: 1 enfant sans descendance.

She is in this record twice over. Her parents, Noël Simard dit Lombrette and Madeleine Racine, are already ancestors of this family — but on the other side, through their son Joseph, down the Simard, Tanguay and LaRochelle lines to Marion Audette and so to Lillian Tremblay. Joseph was her brother.

So in 1683 the Tremblay line married into the Simards and the connection died with her inside two years. The Simards reached this family anyway, by an entirely separate route, arriving through Marion Audette two hundred and forty years later. She is the near miss.

bio.t: A great-grandson of John Joseph Foley and Isabella Gore, born at Pawtucket in 1942. He served as a captain in the United States Air Force and then spent his career in the Federal Bureau of Investigation, retiring from it.
Around 1966 he married Mary McConahey of Concordia, Kansas. Six children: Sean, Ann, Tim, Cary, Ryan and Brady.
He died on 1 November 2024 and is buried at Miramar National Cemetery in San Diego.

His is the most recent death recorded anywhere in this tree, and he is the furthest west any Foley in it travelled. Five generations from a carpenter’s house at Newcastle West to a national cemetery on the Pacific.

benson_kevin.name: Kevin Benson
vitals: 1920 US census — in Alonzo and Josephine Benson’s household, aged 10

bio.t: A brother nobody in this family has mentioned. The 1920 federal census records a son named Kevin, aged ten, in Alonzo and Josephine Benson’s household. He is in no later return: not 1930, not 1940, not 1950.

He appears in no obituary either. Alonzo’s of 1955 names three sons, Harry, Lewis and Horace, and one daughter. Lucy Goldsborough’s of 1948 names her surviving children without him. Nobody living has spoken of him.

That pattern usually means a death in childhood or adolescence between 1920 and 1930, of the kind families stop mentioning. But it is inference. A Massachusetts death record for a Kevin Benson in that decade would settle it, and Attleboro burial records would too.
Found by John Brennan in July 2026, more than a century after the return was filed. He is the only person in this record known to have existed and otherwise entirely unaccounted for.
She brought the libel for divorce in 1960, on grounds of desertion and neglect, while Harry was living in California and she remained in Attleboro with a minor child.
She outlived the marriage by forty-three years and died in 2003, five years before Harry.

esther_kelly.name: Esther Kelly
vitals: 18 September 1937, Grave 58, Section D, St Mary’s Plot, Dean’s Grange Cemetery, Blackrock
£1 2s 6d — one pound for the interment, two and six for dressing the grave
John (Eoin) O’Keeffe, through J. J. Connolly Esq., P.C., of Blackrock
Dean’s Grange Joint Burial Board, no. 49469

bio.t: She kept house for Eoin O’Keeffe. When she died in 1937 he paid for her funeral and her grave, and the receipt survives among his papers.
One pound two shillings and sixpence, to the Dean’s Grange Joint Burial Board, on 18 September 1937. Grave Space 58, Section D, St Mary’s Plot.

The printed note at the foot of the receipt explains what he had bought and what he had not. These were unpurchased graves: residents within the Rathdown Union Area had four years from the first interment to buy third or fourth class grave spaces, and those outside had one year, after which the grave becomes the property of the Board.

She is in this record for the same reason William Graham is. Neither is related to anyone in it. Both are here because somebody in this family decided that a person who would otherwise have gone unrecorded should not. He paid to bury his housekeeper; he and Miriam later raised a stone over a stranger in his great-grandmother’s grave.
